title: IB History Common Mistakes and How to Avoid Them
summary: IB History common mistakes can cost easy marks. Learn to read command terms, use precise evidence, structure answers, and manage timing under pressure.
body_markdown:
Imagine a capable IB History student called Maya. She knows the chronology, remembers the major leaders and can explain why events unfolded. Yet when her marked practice exam returns, the result is lower than expected.


The problem was not a lack of knowledge. Maya evaluated when the question asked her to compare, mentioned evidence without making it precise and spent so long perfecting her first response that the final one became a rushed outline.


Maya is hypothetical, but the pattern is familiar. Many **IB History common mistakes** are not knowledge failures. They are execution failures. The most effective solution is to practise identifying the exact task, selecting relevant evidence and completing answers under realistic time pressure.


One important note: IB History students taking examinations through 2027 follow the current course, while the revised course is first assessed in May 2028. Always check the assessment format and timing for your own cohort with your teacher.


### A quick mistake-prevention checklist


Before writing, ask yourself:


- What does the command term require me to do?
- What people, places, periods or course units must I address?
- What precise evidence will support each claim?
- Am I analysing causes, consequences, similarities or significance rather than narrating events?
- How much time can I give this answer?
- Have I reserved time to complete every required response?


The checklist is short because it needs to work when the clock is loud and your memory feels crowded. For a broader preparation framework, use this[guide to preparing for IB History exams](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/how-to-prepare-for-ib-history-exams-a-comprehensive-guide) .


### Mistake: misreading the command term


A student can write an intelligent essay and still answer the wrong question. This is one of the most expensive errors because everything that follows may be historically accurate but insufficiently relevant.


Consider the difference between these tasks:


- **Compare and contrast** requires sustained attention to similarities and differences.
- **Evaluate** requires a supported judgment about value, importance or validity.
- **Discuss** requires a balanced consideration of arguments or perspectives.
- **To what extent** requires a clear position about the degree to which a claim is convincing.


Maya saw a familiar topic and began writing everything she knew. She treated recognition as understanding. But the examiner does not reward the amount of remembered material in isolation. The response must meet the precise demands of the question.


### The fix: translate before you write


Underline the command term, circle the subject and mark any scope words. Then rewrite the task mentally as an instruction.


For example, a comparison question becomes: “I must make direct comparisons throughout, not write two separate biographies.” An evaluation question becomes: “I must establish criteria, weigh evidence and reach a reasoned judgment.”


Build your thesis from that translation. If the command term disappeared from your planning, it will probably disappear from your essay too. RevisionDojo’s[IB History essay structure guide](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/ib-history-essay-structure-7-worthy-response) explains how to keep an argument aligned from introduction to conclusion.


A student brings everything they know to an exam while the question asks for something narrower


### Mistake: missing part of the required scope


“Missing units” in History does not usually mean forgetting a measurement. It means overlooking part of the question’s required territory, such as a second case, another region, a specified period or one side of a comparison.


A student might write convincingly about one leader when the question requires two. Another might discuss political consequences while ignoring the social consequences named in the prompt. These answers can look substantial while remaining incomplete.


This often happens because students choose a question based on one familiar phrase. Maya recognised her strongest topic, started immediately and noticed the second requirement only near the end.


### The fix: turn the question into scope boxes


Before planning, divide the prompt into visible components. A question requiring two states and both domestic and foreign factors creates four checks:


- State A, domestic factors
- State A, foreign factors
- State B, domestic factors
- State B, foreign factors


The boxes do not need equal space, but none should vanish accidentally. If your course uses different prescribed subjects or regional requirements, follow the wording and rules for your assessment version.


Good revision also needs to match what you are actually studying. The[best IB History resources for self-study](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/best-ib-history-resources-self-study) can help you choose material with appropriate syllabus coverage rather than collecting generic notes.


### Mistake: using vague or disconnected evidence


History essays need evidence, but more facts do not automatically create a stronger argument. A date, policy or historian’s interpretation earns its place by helping prove the sentence around it.


Weak evidence sounds like this: “The policy caused major opposition.” Better evidence identifies the policy, relevant actors, period and consequence. The strongest version also explains why that evidence supports the argument being made.


Students commonly lose precision in three ways:


- They make broad claims without a named example.
- They add memorised facts that do not answer the question.
- They present evidence and move on without explaining its significance.


### The fix: connect claim, evidence and reasoning


Use a simple internal test for each paragraph:


**Claim:** What am I arguing?


**Evidence:** What specific historical detail supports it?


**Reasoning:** Why does that detail prove the claim, and how important is it compared with another factor?


You do not need to force a quotation or date into every sentence. Accuracy and relevance matter more than decorative detail. RevisionDojo[Study Notes](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/best-ib-history-resources-self-study) can rebuild understanding, while Flashcards can help retrieve names, dates, policies and examples. AI Chat can then test whether you can explain why those details matter rather than merely recognise them.


### Mistake: narrating instead of analysing


Narrative tells the reader what happened next. Analysis explains why it happened, why it mattered and how strongly it supports an argument.


Chronology is useful, but an essay organised only as a timeline can become descriptive. The student remains busy recounting events while the judgment waits until the conclusion. By then, the argument has had little room to develop.


### The fix: make every paragraph answer the question


Start paragraphs with analytical claims rather than events. Compare factors, question their relative importance and acknowledge limits. Useful prompts include:


- Why was this factor more significant than another?
- Did its importance change over time?
- Was this a cause, a condition or a trigger?
- Does the evidence support the argument in every case?


The conclusion should synthesize judgments already established, not introduce analysis that the body omitted. If this remains difficult, the article on[why students struggle with IB History](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/why-students-struggle-with-ib-history-and-how-revisiondojo-helps-first-assessment-2028) offers a useful way to diagnose the gap between content knowledge and exam performance.


### Mistake: letting timing decide the result


Maya’s first answer was polished. Her final response was unfinished. The trade looked sensible in the moment because improving a paragraph feels productive, while moving on feels uncomfortable.


But examination marks are distributed across the required tasks. Extra minutes spent refining one answer can become missing analysis elsewhere. Timing is therefore not an administrative detail. It shapes what the examiner is able to reward.


### The fix: budget by task and practise stopping


Work backwards from your assessment’s official duration. Reserve a short planning period for each extended response and protect time for every required task. Set a firm stopping point, even when an answer feels imperfect.


Then practise the transition itself. When time is called, finish the sentence, record any final judgment briefly and move on. This habit is difficult to build through untimed revision because notes do not create the emotional pressure of leaving an answer behind.


RevisionDojo’s[IB History study techniques](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/best-study-techniques-for-ib-history-hl-students-study-smarter-not-harder) can help you combine retrieval, writing and review. Predicted Papers and Mock Exams can also create longer practice sessions, while Tutors can identify where your time is producing the fewest marks.


### Turn IB History examiner reports into actions


**IB History examiner reports** are most useful when treated as diagnostic material, not as a list of warnings. Their observations vary by session and course version, so check that any report matches your assessment. Then convert each relevant comment into a behaviour you can practise.


If feedback warns about descriptive responses, rewrite one paragraph around a comparative judgment. If it highlights weak supporting knowledge, create a compact evidence bank. If candidates frequently misread a task, practise annotating prompts before writing anything.


The[guide to what IB examiner reports reward](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/ib-examiner-reports-what-they-reward) can help you translate broad feedback into concrete changes. RevisionDojo’s Coursework Library and Grading tools can provide additional models and feedback, but the goal is not to copy a polished answer. It is to understand the decisions that made the answer effective.


### Make easy marks harder to lose


Maya did not need another hundred pages of notes. She needed a smaller, more honest practice loop: attempt, diagnose, repair and repeat.


Start with the RevisionDojo **Questionbank** . Choose prompts that expose one weakness at a time, whether that is command terms, evidence or analysis. Review your answer with grading feedback, keep a mistake log and repeat the task until the correction becomes automatic.


Then sit timed papers in **Exam mode** . This is where planning, scope and stopping rules become real rather than theoretical. For cohort-specific preparation, the[May 2028 IB History study advice](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/may-2028-ib-history-study-advice) also explains how to connect Questionbank practice, Predicted Papers and Mock Exams.


Knowledge still matters. But marks are awarded for what you do with knowledge under the conditions of the assessment. The best IB History exam tips therefore begin with a simple principle: do not merely revise the subject. Rehearse the decisions the exam will require.
